mainTopic: מומים of a כהן (eyes, body proportion, ears, lips, teeth) and related blemishes in animals: unusual horns and damaged horns and hooves.
overview: This amud begins by finishing the discussion of a חרום and then explains the eye מומים of a כהן. The גמרא shows that 'eyes above' and 'eyes below' in the משנה describe where the eyes sit on the face, not the direction he looks. It finds the source for these מומים in the extra word 'בעינו'. A ברייתא teaches that a כהן blind in one eye is an עור, and that the extra word 'איש' adds pale spots and constant tears. רבא then explains why the תורה needs all five eye words: איש, עור, דק, תבלול and בעינו. Each word covers its own kind of eye defect. The גמרא defines more terms from the משנה, such as סכי שמש, זגדיין and הצירן, and settles whether missing eyelashes are a real מום. A new משנה lists blemishes of proportion, of the ears, lips and teeth, which leads to רב's teaching that משה was ten holy אמות tall. The amud ends with animals: which unusual features are not real blemishes, and how horns and hooves that were cut or uprooted affect whether an animal is fit and whether it may be redeemed.

steps.title: Closing line of the חרום discussion
steps.stepSummary: The previous discussion ends: a כהן with a sunken nose counts as a חרום even if he cannot paint both eyes in one stroke.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, even if he does not paint both of his eyes at once, he is a חרום.
steps.whatsHappening: We are joining at the very end of the previous discussion. These words finish the גמרא's point about the מום called חרום.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier, the sign of a חרום was that he could paint both eyes in a single stroke, because the bridge of his nose is so low. Here the גמרא says this sign is not required. Any abnormally sunken nose already counts as the מום.

keyTerms.meaning: A כהן with an abnormally sunken or flat nose, which is a מום
At once; together, in one motion

steps.confusionAlert: This line starts in the middle of a sentence. The main claim that it finishes came at the end of the previous עמוד, so do not try to read it as a new topic.

phrases.english: even though he does not paint
both of his eyes at once.

steps.triggerLanguage: אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁאֵינוֹ כּוֹחֵל שְׁתֵּי עֵינָיו כְּאַחַת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the חרום discussion carried over from the previous עמוד.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Broadening the definition: the stroke test is not required.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Only a כהן who can paint both eyes in one stroke counts as a חרום.
steps.terutzMaskana: Any abnormally sunken nose counts as חרום, even without that sign.

steps.title: What do 'eyes above' and 'eyes below' mean?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה and asks what is meant by a כהן whose eyes are 'above' or 'below'.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה says: 'Both of his eyes are below.' What does the משנה mean by 'both of his eyes are above' and 'both of his eyes are below'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes a new line from the משנה and asks what it means. This sets up the next move, where the גמרא tries out one explanation.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words 'up' and 'down' are unclear. They could describe the direction he looks, or the place where his eyes sit on his face. The question asks which one the משנה means.

phrases.english: Both of his eyes below.
phrases.notes: A quote from the משנה, used as a heading.

phrases.english: What is 'both of his eyes above'
and 'both of his eyes below'?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic: the next מום in the משנה.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether 'above' and 'below' describe the direction he looks or the position of the eyes.

steps.title: If it means looking direction, one case is a repeat
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests the phrases describe where he looks, then shows this makes the 'one up, one down' case the same as the משנה's next case.
steps.simpleTranslation: Suppose 'both eyes above' means he looks upward and 'both eyes below' means he looks downward. Then 'one eye above and one eye below' would mean one eye looks down and one eye looks up. But that is exactly the משנה's next case, 'he sees the room and the upper story at once'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries one explanation: the משנה is talking about the direction of his gaze. It then knocks this explanation down.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the cases describe gaze, then 'one up, one down' means each eye looks in a different direction. That is the same thing as 'seeing the lower room and the upper story together', which the משנה lists as its own case. The משנה would not list the same מום twice, so this reading must be wrong.

keyTerms.meaning: If you say; suppose it means (introduces a reading the גמרא will reject)
The ground-floor room and the upper story

steps.confusionAlert: The proposed reading is not rejected because it is illogical. It is rejected because it would make the משנה say the same thing twice.

phrases.english: If you say: both of his eyes above —
means that he looks upward,
both of his eyes below — that he looks downward,

phrases.aramaic: עֵינוֹ אַחַת לְמַעְלָה וְעֵינוֹ אַחַת לְמַטָּה —
phrases.english: one eye above and one eye below —
means he looks with one eye downward
and one eye upward,
but that is the same as 'he sees the room'
'and the upper story at once'!

steps.triggerLanguage: אִילֵּימָא שְׁתֵּי עֵינָיו לְמַעְלָה דְּחָזֵי לְמַעְלָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tries out a first answer to the question and refutes it.
steps.kashyaTarget: The reading that 'above' and 'below' describe the direction of his gaze.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Redundancy: on this reading, the 'one up, one down' case is identical to the separate case of seeing the room and the upper story at once.

steps.title: It means where the eyes physically sit
steps.stepSummary: The phrases describe the physical position of the eyes on the face. Seeing the room and the upper story together is a separate case, where the eyes sit normally.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, 'both eyes above' means his eyes are set higher than normal, and 'both eyes below' means they are set lower than normal. 'One eye above and one eye below' means one is set high and one is set low. Then there is a separate case: his eyes are in their normal places, but he still sees the room and the upper story at once.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the correct explanation: the משנה describes where the eyes are located on the face, not where he looks.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now every case in the משנה is different from the others. Three cases are about eyes placed in the wrong spot. The 'room and upper story' case is about a כהן whose eyes are placed normally but who looks in two directions at once. The repetition problem from the previous step disappears.

keyTerms.meaning: In their normal order or position

steps.whatToRemember: 'Up' and 'down' in this משנה describe where the eyes sit on the face. Looking in two directions at once with normally placed eyes is a separate מום.

phrases.english: Rather: both of his eyes above —
means they are positioned high,
both of his eyes below — they are positioned low,

phrases.aramaic: עֵינוֹ אַחַת לְמַעְלָה וְעֵינוֹ אַחַת לְמַטָּה —
phrases.english: one eye above and one eye below —
means one eye is positioned high
and one eye is positioned low,
and also where they are positioned normally,

phrases.aramaic: וְרוֹאֶה אֶת הַחֶדֶר וְאֶת הָעֲלִיָּיה כְּאַחַת.
phrases.english: but he sees the room and the upper story at once.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא, שְׁתֵּי עֵינָיו לְמַעְלָה דְּקָיְימָן לְמַעְלָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces the rejected gaze reading with a reading about physical position.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterpreting the wording of the משנה.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'Above' and 'below' describe the direction of his gaze.
steps.terutzMaskana: They describe where the eyes are placed. Gazing two ways at once is a distinct case, with the eyes in their normal places.

steps.title: What is the source for these eye מומים?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks where these eye מומים come from in the תורה.
steps.simpleTranslation: From where do we learn these things?
steps.whatsHappening: Now that the cases are defined, the גמרא asks for their source in the תורה. This sets up the ברייתא that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה lists these eye problems as מומים, but none of them is stated clearly in the פסוק. The גמרא wants to know what in the פסוק tells us about them.

keyTerms.meaning: From where are these words (derived)? A standard request for a source

phrases.english: From where are these matters derived?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from defining the cases to asking for their source.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which פסוק teaches that these eye conditions are מומים.

steps.title: A ברייתא learns them from the word 'בעינו'
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that the extra word 'בעינו' includes every eye defect, including all the cases in the משנה.
steps.simpleTranslation: As the רבנן taught: 'In his eye' teaches that anything wrong in his eye counts. From here they said: both eyes below, both eyes above, one eye above and one eye below, seeing the room and the upper story at once, or when he talks to one person and someone else says, 'He is looking at me.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the source question with a ברייתא. It derives all these eye מומים from the word 'בעינו' in the פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק about the מומים of a כהן says 'או תבלל בעינו'. The word 'בעינו' seems unnecessary, since a תבלל can only be in the eye anyway. So the word is read as including every eye defect. The ברייתא lists the משנה's cases, and adds one more: a person whose gaze is so off that when he talks to one person, someone else thinks he is being looked at.

keyTerms.meaning: In his eye: the word in the פסוק that is used to include all eye defects

steps.whatToRemember: All of these eye מומים come from the inclusive word 'בעינו', meaning anything wrong with the eye. That includes misplaced eyes, eyes that look two ways at once, and a gaze that seems aimed at someone else.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that the list of מומים in the משנה is rooted in the פסוק, through an inclusive reading of one extra word.

phrases.english: As the Sages taught:
'In his eye' — anything that is in his eye,
from here they said:
both of his eyes below,
both of his eyes above,

phrases.aramaic: עֵינוֹ אַחַת לְמַעְלָה וְעֵינוֹ אַחַת לְמַטָּה,
phrases.english: one eye above and one eye below,

phrases.aramaic: וְרוֹאֶה אֶת הַחֶדֶר וְאֶת הָעֲלִיָּיה כְּאֶחָת,
phrases.english: or he sees the room and the upper story at once,
or when he speaks with his friend
and another person says: 'He is looking at me.'

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּתָנוּ רַבָּנַן: בְּעֵינוֹ כׇּל מָה שֶׁבְּעֵינוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the source question directly.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The extra word 'בעינו' in the פסוק includes every eye defect, and the ברייתא lists the משנה's cases plus one more.

steps.title: Blind in one eye counts as blind
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that the word עור includes a כהן blind in only one eye.
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן taught: 'עור' means whether he is blind in both eyes or blind in only one eye.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new ברייתא that explains the word עור in the list of a כהן's מומים. It says blindness in even one eye disqualifies him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Someone might think עור means only total blindness. The ברייתא says one blind eye is enough to count as a מום. This opens a new source discussion about the eye מומים.

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught: 'Blind' —
whether he is blind in both his eyes,
or blind in one of his eyes.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a second ברייתא on the sources for eye מומים, this time explaining the word עור.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Blindness in even one eye disqualifies a כהן as עור.

steps.title: Where do pale spots and constant tears come from?
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא asks for the source that חורוור and constant tearing are מומים.
steps.simpleTranslation: Pale spots on the eye and constant tears: from where do we know they disqualify?
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא asks a question that sets up its next teaching. It wants a תורה source for two eye conditions that are not plain blindness.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In these cases the eye is still there, but vision is blocked. Because the eye is not simply blind, the word עור alone might not include them, so a source is needed.

keyTerms.meaning: Pale or white spots on the eye

phrases.english: Pale spots and constant tears
from where do we know?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After defining עור, the ברייתא asks about related conditions that are not full blindness.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A פסוק source for disqualifying חורוור and constant tears.

steps.title: The extra word 'man' includes them
steps.stepSummary: The word איש in 'איש עור' adds חורוור and constant tears.
steps.simpleTranslation: The verse says: 'A blind man.'
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא answers that the word איש in the פסוק 'איש עור' includes these two conditions.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק could have just said עור. The extra word איש is read as adding cases that are like blindness, where the eye is present but does not see properly.

keyTerms.meaning: Man (the extra word used to include more cases)

phrases.english: The verse states: 'A blind man.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the ברייתא's question from step 8.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The extra word איש in 'איש עור' includes חורוור and constant tears.

steps.title: Why does the תורה need five eye words?
steps.stepSummary: רבא asks why the תורה writes איש, עור, דק, תבלול, and בעינו.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: Why do I need the Merciful One to write 'איש,' 'עור,' 'דק,' 'תבלול,' and 'בעינו'?
steps.whatsHappening: רבא asks why the תורה uses five different words about eye problems. This question sets up his explanation of why each word is needed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If one word could teach everything, the others would seem extra. רבא is not really challenging the תורה. He is preparing to show that each word adds a case the others would miss.

keyTerms.meaning: A film or cataract on the eye
Mixing of the white and black of the eye

phrases.english: Rava said: Why do I need
that the Merciful One wrote
'man,' 'blind,' 'cataract,' 'tevallul,' 'in his eye'?

steps.confusionAlert: This is not a real attack. רבא asks 'why do I need' so that he can explain the need for each word himself.
steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רָבָא: לְמָה לִי דִּכְתַב רַחֲמָנָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the ברייתות used איש and בעינו, רבא asks why all five words are needed.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What each of the five eye words adds that the others do not.

steps.title: 'Blind' alone would miss eyes that are there but cannot see
steps.stepSummary: From עור alone we might think only missing eyes count, so איש adds חורוור and constant tears.
steps.simpleTranslation: They are all needed. If the Merciful One wrote only 'blind,' I would say that is because the eyes are not there at all. But pale spots and constant tears, where the eyes are present, I would say are not a מום. So the Merciful One wrote 'man.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבא begins his answer by showing why איש is needed in addition to עור.
steps.deeperAnalysis: עור might mean only a כהן whose eyes are missing. A כהן with חורוור or constant tears still has his eyes, so we might think he is fine. איש teaches that he is also disqualified.

keyTerms.meaning: They are needed (each word is necessary)
They (the eyes) are not there at all

phrases.english: They are necessary, for if the Merciful One had written 'blind'
I would say that is because the eyes are not there at all,
but pale spots and constant tears,
where the eyes are still in him — not,
so the Merciful One wrote 'man.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins answering רבא's question with the first link of the צריכותא.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: איש is needed to include eyes that are present but blocked (חורוור and constant tears), which עור alone might exclude.

steps.title: 'Man' alone would miss weak vision
steps.stepSummary: From איש we might think only total loss of sight counts, so דק adds weakened vision.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if the Merciful One wrote only 'man,' I would say that is because he does not see at all. But weakened vision I would say is not a מום. So the Merciful One wrote 'cataract.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבא continues the chain and shows why דק is needed in addition to איש.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The cases included by איש still involve no sight at all. A כהן who sees, but poorly, might seem fine. דק teaches that weakened vision is also a מום.

keyTerms.meaning: He does not see at all

phrases.english: And if the Merciful One had written 'man' —
I would say that is because he does not see at all,
but weakened vision — not,
so the Merciful One wrote 'cataract.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Next link in the צריכותא, moving from no sight to weak sight.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: דק is needed to include weakened vision, which איש alone might exclude.

steps.title: 'Cataract' alone would miss mixed-up eyes
steps.stepSummary: From דק we might think only reduced vision counts, so תבלול adds eyes whose colors are mixed.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if the Merciful One wrote only 'דק,' I would say that is because the vision is reduced. But mixed eyes I would say are not a מום. So the Merciful One wrote 'תבלול.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבא continues and shows why תבלול is needed in addition to דק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: דק is about vision that is reduced. With תבלול, the white and black parts of the eye run into each other, even if vision is not clearly weaker. תבלול teaches that this is also a מום.

keyTerms.meaning: They (the eyes) are lacking or reduced
Mixed-up eyes (white and black run together)

phrases.english: And if the Merciful One had written 'cataract' —
I would say that is because the vision is reduced,
but mixed-up eyes — not,
so the Merciful One wrote 'tevallul.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Next link in the צריכותא, moving from weak vision to mixed eyes.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: תבלול is needed to include mixed eyes, which דק alone might exclude.

steps.title: 'תבלול' alone would miss eyes that only look different
steps.stepSummary: From תבלול we might think only mixed eyes count, so בעינו adds any unusual eye, even with normal vision.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if the Merciful One wrote only 'תבלול,' I would say that is because the eyes are mixed. But just because the eye looks different, I would say it is not a מום. So the Merciful One wrote 'בעינו.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבא finishes the chain by showing why בעינו is needed. It includes eyes that only look unusual, like the high or low eyes from the משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The last case has no vision problem and no mixing at all. The eye just looks different from normal. בעינו teaches that even this is a מום, which fits step 6, where בעינו includes every eye defect in the משנה.

keyTerms.meaning: An unusual look (eyes that differ from normal)

phrases.english: And if the Merciful One had written 'tevallul' —
I would say that is because the eyes are mixed,
but because of an unusual appearance — not,
so the Merciful One wrote 'in his eye.'

steps.whatToRemember: Each word reaches one step further. עור covers missing eyes. איש covers eyes that are there but cannot see. דק covers weak vision. תבלול covers mixed eyes. בעינו covers eyes that just look different.
steps.whyThisMatters: This explains why the משנה's purely physical cases, like eyes set too high or too low, count as מומים even when the כהן sees perfectly.
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Final link in the צריכותא, completing רבא's answer.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: בעינו is needed to include eyes that only look different, which תבלול alone might exclude.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: All five words are needed. Together they cover every level of eye defect, from missing eyes to eyes that only look unusual.

steps.title: רבא sums up which word teaches which eye blemish
steps.stepSummary: רבא concludes that each eye-word in the פסוק covers its own family of blemishes: dimness from איש, weak vision from דק, mixed eyes from תבלול, and unusual-looking eyes from בעינו.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: Therefore, every blemish caused by dimness of sight comes from the word "איש". Blemishes of weakened vision come from "דק". Blemishes where the parts of the eye are mixed together come from "תבלול". Blemishes where the eye just looks different come from "בעינו".
steps.whatsHappening: רבא wraps up his explanation of why the תורה needed all these words. He now gives a simple chart of which word is the source for which kind of eye blemish.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In steps 11–14 רבא showed that each word adds something the earlier word could not teach. Here he turns that into a clear rule: every eye blemish belongs to one of four groups, and each group has its own source word. No word in the פסוק is extra.

keyTerms.meaning: Therefore. It introduces a summary or conclusion.
Dimness of the eyes, loss of sight
Mixed or blended parts of the eye
An eye that looks different or unusual

steps.whatToRemember: Four groups of eye blemishes, four source words: איש = dimness, דק = weak vision, תבלול = mixed eye, בעינו = any unusual-looking eye.

phrases.english: Rava said: Therefore,
all blemishes due to dimness of sight come from "man" (איש),
those of weakened vision come from "thin" (דק),
those where the eye is mixed come from "tevallul" (תבלול),
those where the eye looks different come from "in his eye" (בעינו).

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Sums up the four-part answer of steps 11–14 into one organized rule.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Each eye-word in the פסוק is the source for one distinct category of eye blemish.

steps.title: Reading 'סכי שמש' as 'סני שמש', those who hate the sun
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה's term סכי שמש, and רב יוסף teaches the reading סני שמש, people who cannot stand sunlight.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה says "סכי שמש". רב יוסף taught it as "סני שמש", meaning people who "hate the sun" and cannot open their eyes in sunlight.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now moves on to explain specific words in the משנה, starting with סכי שמש. רב יוסף gives a slightly different reading that makes the meaning clear.
steps.deeperAnalysis: סכי could be misunderstood as 'looking at the sun'. רב יוסף's version, סני ('hate'), shows that the blemish is the opposite: the person's eyes cannot handle the sun, so he squints or shuts them.

keyTerms.meaning: The term in the משנה for someone with a sun-related eye problem
He taught (a version of the text)
Hates the sun, cannot look into sunlight

steps.confusionAlert: Do not read סכי שמש as 'one who looks at the sun'. The point is that he cannot look at it.

phrases.english: "Sakhei shemesh" (from the mishna).
Rav Yosef taught: "Sanei shemesh", those who hate the sun.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the פסוק analysis and begins explaining individual terms in the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: סכי שמש means one whose eyes cannot tolerate sunlight (סני שמש).

steps.title: רב הונא shows what 'different eyes' means
steps.stepSummary: To explain זגדיין, רב הונא pointed and said it means one eye like ours and one like theirs. רב יהודה, whose eyes were like that, was offended.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה says "זגדיין". רב הונא demonstrated by pointing: one eye is like ours and one is like theirs. רב יהודה took offense.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the משנה's term זגדיין through רב הונא, who shows that it means two eyes that do not match. The story adds that רב יהודה felt pointed at and was hurt.
steps.deeperAnalysis: According to רב הונא, זגדיין is about the eyes themselves being mismatched, for example in color. The detail that רב יהודה was offended tells us he had this feature, so רב הונא's demonstration felt personal.

keyTerms.meaning: One whose eyes are different from each other
He showed or demonstrated, by pointing

phrases.english: "Zagdeyan": one whose eyes are different (from the mishna).
Rav Huna demonstrated by pointing:
one eye like ours and one like theirs,
and Rav Yehuda took offense.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues explaining terms of the משנה, moving to the next one, זגדיין.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: זגדיין means a person whose two eyes do not match each other.

steps.title: A ברייתא seems to define 'זגדום' as mismatched eyebrows
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that defines זגדום as one eyebrow black and one white. That seems to contradict רב הונא, who said it is about the eyes.
steps.simpleTranslation: They challenged him from a ברייתא: A שכבנא is someone whose eyebrows lie flat over his eyes. A זגדום is someone with one black eyebrow and one white eyebrow.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רב הונא with a ברייתא. The ברייתא links זגדום to the eyebrows, not to the eyes.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא is talking about eyebrows (it begins with שכבנא, whose eyebrows droop) and says זגדום is a black and white eyebrow pair. If זגדום means mismatched eyebrows, רב הונא's explanation about mismatched eyes seems wrong.

keyTerms.meaning: They challenged, from a תנאי source
One whose eyebrows lie flat and droop over his eyes
A mismatched pair (here, one black and one white eyebrow)

phrases.english: They raised an objection: A shekhavna is one whose eyebrows lie flat,
a zagdum is one with one eyebrow black and one white.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks רב הונא's definition of זגדיין from step 17.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב הונא's explanation that זגדיין refers to mismatched eyes
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A ברייתא uses זגדום for mismatched eyebrows, which suggests the term is about eyebrows and not eyes.

steps.title: Any mismatched pair is called 'זגדום'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the ברייתא's תנא uses זגדום for any pair that does not match, so it covers both eyebrows and eyes.
steps.simpleTranslation: The תנא of that ברייתא calls any pair that is not the same as each other "זגדום".
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא resolves the challenge. זגדום is a general word for any mismatched pair, so mismatched eyebrows and mismatched eyes can both be called by it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא was not limiting the word to eyebrows. It used eyebrows as one example of a broader idea, a pair that does not match. רב הונא's use of the word for mismatched eyes therefore still stands.

phrases.aramaic: תַּנָּא: כֹּל זוּגָא דְּלָא שָׁוֵי לַהֲדָדֵי,
phrases.english: The tanna: any pair that is not equal to each other,
he calls it "zagdum".

steps.triggerLanguage: תַּנָּא: כֹּל זוּגָא דְּלָא שָׁוֵי לַהֲדָדֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 18 and defends רב הונא.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Broadening the term: the word is general, not limited to one body part
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא seemed to say זגדום means only mismatched eyebrows.
steps.terutzMaskana: זגדום means any mismatched pair, which includes eyes, so רב הונא is correct.
steps.whatToRemember: זגדום / זגדיין = any pair (eyes or eyebrows) where the two sides do not match.

steps.title: Defining 'הצירן': eyes that droop, are round, or run with tears
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה's term הצירן and lists what it includes: drooping eyelids, round eyes, and eyes that tear, drip, or stream.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה says "הצירן". This means his eyes droop, or are round, or tear, or drip, or stream heavily.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the next term from the משנה, הצירן, by listing the different eye conditions it covers.
steps.deeperAnalysis: הצירן is not one condition. It is a group: eyelids that droop and only partly open, round eyes, and several levels of tearing, from tears to dripping to heavy streaming. Each of these disqualifies a כהן.

keyTerms.meaning: One with problem eyes (drooping or constantly tearing)

phrases.english: "Ha-tzayran" (from the mishna): his eyes droop,
or are round; they tear, drip, or stream heavily.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After resolving זגדיין, the גמרא moves to the next term of the משנה, הצירן.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: הצירן includes drooping eyelids, round eyes, and eyes that tear, drip, or stream.

steps.title: A ברייתא Lists Three Eye and Eyelash Blemishes
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא lists זדיר, לופין, and תימין and defines each one.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was taught: the זדיר, the לופין, and the תימין are blemished. A זויר is one whose eyes look strange. A לופין is one with a lot of eyelashes. A תימין is one whose eyelashes are gone.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes a ברייתא that adds three more blemishes connected to the eyes, and explains what each word means.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This continues the list of eye blemishes from the previous steps. The new idea is that the eyelashes count too. Having too many eyelashes (לופין) or none at all (תימין) is listed as a blemish.

phrases.english: It was taught: the zadir, and the lupin, and the timyan.
phrases.notes: The words in parentheses are the old printed text. The words in brackets are the corrected reading.

phrases.english: Zavir: one whose eyes are strange,
Lupin: one whose eyelashes are many,
Timyan: one whose eyelashes are used up (gone).

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the list of eye blemishes after הצירן.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: זדיר, לופין, and תימין are listed as blemishes.

steps.title: Missing Eyelashes Seem to Be Only an Appearance Problem
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the ברייתא. A משנה says a כהן whose eyelashes fell out is disqualified only because of מראית העין, not as a real blemish.
steps.simpleTranslation: Does the תנא really list these together with real blemishes? But we learned in a משנה: one whose eyelashes fell out is disqualified only because of how it looks!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks how the ברייתא can list תימין (no eyelashes) as a full blemish, when a משנה treats lost eyelashes as only an appearance problem.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There are two levels of disqualification. A real מום is one level. Being disqualified only because of מראית העין is a lighter level. The משנה puts lost eyelashes in the lighter level, but the ברייתא seems to put them in the real-blemish list.

keyTerms.meaning: But didn't we learn in a משנה?
How it looks to others (not a true blemish)

phrases.english: And are these taught together with real blemishes?
But didn't we learn in a mishna:
One whose eyelashes fell out is disqualified
because of how it looks!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָנֵי גַּבֵּי מוּמִין תָּנוּ לְהוּ? וְהָתְנַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the ברייתא's listing of תימין as a real blemish.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's inclusion of תימין among true blemishes.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A משנה rules that lost eyelashes disqualify only because of מראית העין. So they should not appear in a list of true blemishes.

steps.title: It Depends on Whether the Roots Remain
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the two sources speak about different cases: whether or not the roots of the eyelashes remain.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is not difficult. This case is where the roots remain. That case is where the roots do not remain.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא resolves the contradiction by explaining that each source is talking about a different situation.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the eyelash roots are still there, it is only an appearance problem, and that is the משנה. If no roots remain at all, it is a real blemish, and that is the ברייתא. So both sources are correct, each in its own case.
steps.whatToRemember: Lost eyelashes with the roots still there = only מראית העין. No roots left = a true מום.

phrases.english: It is not difficult,
this is where the roots remain,
phrases.notes: The משנה: this is only an appearance problem.

phrases.english: that is where the roots do not remain.
phrases.notes: The ברייתא: this is a real blemish.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 22.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא and the משנה seemed to describe the same case with different rulings.
steps.terutzMaskana: The משנה speaks about roots that remain (מראית העין). The ברייתא speaks about no roots left (a real מום).

steps.title: משנה: Odd-Sized Eyes, Body, or Nose
steps.stepSummary: A new משנה lists blemishes of proportion: eyes too big or too small, and a body or nose out of proportion to the limbs.
steps.simpleTranslation: If his eyes are big like a calf's or small like a goose's; if his body is too big or too small for his limbs; if his nose is too big or too small for his limbs, he is blemished.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins and lists more blemishes. All of them are about parts of the body being the wrong size compared to the rest.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The idea is proportion. A part may be normal in itself and still count as a blemish when it does not match the rest of the body. Keep the body-to-limbs rule in mind, because the גמרא will soon use it.

keyTerms.meaning: His body is too large for his limbs

phrases.english: MISHNA: His eyes are large like those of a calf,
or small like those of a goose.
His body is large compared to his limbs,
or small compared to his limbs.
His nose is large compared to his limbs,
or small compared to his limbs.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new משנה with a new list of blemishes.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Eyes, body, or nose that are out of proportion are blemishes.

steps.title: משנה: The צומם and the צומע (Ear Blemishes)
steps.stepSummary: The משנה lists צומם and צומע and defines them. צומע has small ears. צומם has spongy ears.
steps.simpleTranslation: The צומם and the צומע. What is a צומע? Anyone whose ears are small. And the צומם? Anyone whose ears look like a sponge.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה continues its list with two ear blemishes, and explains what each name means.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה itself defines the two terms, so we do not need the גמרא to explain them. One is about ears that are too small. The other is about ears that are shaped strangely, like a sponge.

phrases.english: The tzomem and the tzomea:
Which is a tzomea?
Anyone whose ears are small,
and the tzomem: anyone whose ears look like a sponge.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the משנה's list.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Small ears (צומע) and sponge-like ears (צומם) are blemishes.

steps.title: משנה: Uneven Lips and Missing Teeth
steps.stepSummary: Uneven lips are a real blemish. Missing teeth disqualify only because of מראית העין.
steps.simpleTranslation: If his upper lip sticks out past the lower, or the lower past the upper, that is a blemish. And one whose teeth fell out is disqualified because of how it looks.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה ends its list with lips that stick out and teeth that fell out.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Notice the two levels again. Uneven lips are called a true מום (הרי זה מום). Missing teeth are only disqualified because of מראית העין, like lost eyelashes in step 22.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up the two rulings. Lips = a real מום. Missing teeth = disqualified only because of how it looks.

phrases.english: His upper lip sticks out past the lower,
or the lower sticks out past the upper:
this is a blemish.
And one whose teeth fell out:
is disqualified because of how it looks.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the משנה's list.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Uneven lips are a מום. Missing teeth disqualify because of מראית העין.

steps.title: רב: משה רבינו Was Ten אמות Tall
steps.stepSummary: רב proves from פסוקים that משה was ten אמות tall: he spread the tent over the משכן, whose boards were ten אמות high.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב said: משה our teacher was ten אמות tall, as it says, 'And he spread the tent over the משכן.' Who spread it? משה spread it. And it is written, 'Ten אמות is the length of a board.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins with רב's teaching about how tall משה was. It is connected to the משנה's rule about body size.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The proof works in two steps. First, משה personally spread the covering over the משכן. Second, the משכן's boards were ten אמות tall. So משה must have been at least ten אמות tall to reach over them.

phrases.english: GEMARA: Rav said:
Moshe our teacher was ten amos tall,
as it says: 'And he spread the tent over the Mishkan.'
Who spread it? Moshe our teacher spread it,
and it is written: 'Ten amos is the length of a board.'

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב: מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ עֶשֶׂר אַמּוֹת הָיָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a teaching connected to the משנה's rule about body size.

steps.title: רב שימי: That Would Make משה Blemished
steps.stepSummary: רב שימי בר חייא objects that ten אמות would make משה's body out of proportion to his limbs, which the משנה calls a blemish.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב שימי בר חייא said to רב: If so, you have made משה our teacher a בעל מום! For we learned: his body is large or small compared to his limbs.
steps.whatsHappening: רב שימי בר חייא attacks רב's statement using the משנה we just learned.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A normal person is about three of his own arm-lengths (אמות) tall. If משה was ten of his own אמות, his body would be far too big for his arms. That is exactly the blemish of גופו גדול מאבריו.

keyTerms.meaning: As we learned in a משנה

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב שִׁימִי בַּר חִיָּיא לְרַב:
phrases.english: Rav Shimi bar Chiya said to Rav:

phrases.aramaic: אִם כֵּן עֲשִׂיתוֹ לְמֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ בַּעַל מוּם!
phrases.english: If so, you have made Moshe our teacher a blemished person!
For we learned:

phrases.aramaic: גּוּפוֹ גָּדוֹל מֵאֵבָרָיו אוֹ קָטָן מֵאֵבָרָיו.
phrases.english: His body is large compared to his limbs or small compared to his limbs.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִם כֵּן עֲשִׂיתוֹ לְמֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ בַּעַל מוּם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רב's statement in step 27.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב's claim that משה was ten אמות tall.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If 'ten אמות' means ten of משה's own arm-lengths, his body would be out of proportion to his limbs, which the משנה calls a מום.

steps.title: רב: I Meant the Holy אמה
steps.stepSummary: רב answers that he meant ten of the standard holy אמות used in the משכן, not ten of משה's own arm-lengths.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: שימי! I was speaking about the אמה של קודש.
steps.whatsHappening: רב explains which measuring unit he meant, and this removes the problem.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The אמה של קודש is the fixed measure used for the משכן. It is not the length of משה's own arm. So משה could be ten of those אמות tall and still have arms in proper proportion to his body.

keyTerms.meaning: The holy cubit, the standard measure used for the משכן

steps.confusionAlert: The question used 'אמה' to mean משה's own arm. רב's answer uses 'אמה' to mean a fixed holy measurement. The whole answer depends on this difference.
steps.whatToRemember: משה was ten standard holy אמות tall and perfectly proportioned, so he was not a בעל מום.

phrases.english: He said to him: Shimi!
I was speaking of the holy amah.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רב שימי's קשיא.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Ten אמות meant ten of משה's own arm-lengths, which would be out of proportion.
steps.terutzMaskana: It means ten standard holy אמות, so משה's limbs were in proportion to his body.

steps.title: How big is a 'large nose'
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא gives the size for the משנה's 'large nose' blemish: the size of a little finger.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: 'His nose is large, etc.' A ברייתא taught: the measure is like a little finger.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the משנה's 'large nose' blemish and brings a ברייתא that gives it an exact size.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה only said a nose that is too big or too small for the body is a blemish. The ברייתא adds a measurement: the size of a little finger. Without a size, we would not know where 'normal' ends and 'blemish' begins.

phrases.english: His nose is large, etc.
It was taught: like a small finger.
phrases.notes: This is the measure of the difference that counts as a blemish.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back to the משנה's list after the story about משה's height.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A nose that is out of proportion by the size of a little finger is a blemish.

steps.title: A third ear blemish is added
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא adds the צימח to the משנה's two ear blemishes, צומם and צומע.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה listed 'the צומם and the צומע.' A ברייתא taught: the צימח is also a blemish.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the משנה's two ear blemishes. It then brings a ברייתא that adds a third one, the צימח.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה named only two kinds of unusual ears. The ברייתא says there is a third kind that also disqualifies a כהן. But the ברייתא does not say what a צימח is. That gap sets up the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: Another type of unusual ear; explained in the next steps

phrases.english: The tzomem and the tzome'a.
It was taught: also the tzime'ach.
phrases.notes: The ברייתא adds a third ear blemish.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on to the next item in the משנה's list.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A צימח is also a blemish that disqualifies a כהן.

steps.title: The רבנן did not know what the word meant
steps.stepSummary: The רבנן did not know the meaning of the word צימח.
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן did not know what 'צימח' meant.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells us the רבנן did not know what this word meant. This sets up the story that explains it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא used a rare word. Even the חכמים needed to find out what it meant. The question here is about the meaning of a word, not about the law.

phrases.english: The Sages did not know
what 'tzime'ach' is.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Points out the open question left by the ברייתא in step 31.

steps.title: An Arab trader reveals the meaning
steps.stepSummary: The רבנן heard an Arab selling a 'צימח'. It turned out to be a goat with long ears.
steps.simpleTranslation: They heard a certain Arab calling out, 'Who wants a צימח?' It turned out to be a long-eared goat.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question by telling a story. An Arab trader used the word, and the רבנן saw what he was selling.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word was still used in everyday language, so the רבנן learned its meaning from how people spoke. The animal being sold had long ears. So a צימח is someone or something with long ears, the opposite of the צומע's small ears.

keyTerms.meaning: It turned out / it was found

steps.whatToRemember: There are three ear blemishes: צומע (small ears), צומם (spongy ears), and צימח (long ears).

phrases.english: They heard a certain Arab
who was saying:
'Who wants a tzime'ach?'
And it turned out to be a long-eared goat.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question from step 32.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A צימח has long ears, like the goat the Arab was selling.

steps.title: Unusual horns do not disqualify a קרבן
steps.stepSummary: רב חסדא rules that a female goat with no horns and a female lamb with horns are fit for the מזבח.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חסדא said: a female goat that has no horns, and a female lamb that has horns, are fit to be offered on the altar.
steps.whatsHappening: רב חסדא moves from the blemishes of a כהן to animals. He says some unusual features do not make an animal unfit for a קרבן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Female goats normally have horns, and female lambs normally do not. Each animal in his ruling is the opposite of what is normal. Even so, רב חסדא says being different is not the same as being blemished, so these animals may be offered.

keyTerms.meaning: Fit to be offered on the altar

phrases.english: Rav Chisda said:
A female goat that has no horns,
and a female lamb that has horns —
are fit for the altar.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns from the blemishes of a כהן to the related question of blemishes in animals.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A hornless female goat and a horned female lamb are not blemished and may be offered on the מזבח.

steps.title: A ברייתא supports רב חסדא
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא lists features that look like blemishes but are not. These animals may be offered in the מקדש, but a בכור with them may not be slaughtered outside it. The list includes רב חסדא's two cases and the three ear features.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was also taught this way: some things look like blemishes but are not blemishes. We may slaughter animals with them in the מקדש, but not in the rest of the country. These are: a goat with no horns, a lamb with horns, the צימח, the צומם, and the צומע.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that says the same thing as רב חסדא. It also adds the three ear features to the list.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since these are not real blemishes, the animal is fine for a קרבן in the מקדש. For the same reason, a בכור with one of these features cannot be slaughtered and eaten outside the מקדש, because only a real blemish allows that. So one fact, 'not a real blemish,' leads to both results.

keyTerms.meaning: It was also taught this way (a ברייתא that supports the statement)
In the rest of the country (outside the מקדש)

steps.confusionAlert: The same ear features (צומם, צומע, צימח) are real blemishes for a כהן, but not for an animal. Do not mix up the two lists.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that 'not a blemish' works in two directions. It helps (the animal may be a קרבן), and it also limits (a בכור with this feature cannot be slaughtered outside the מקדש).
steps.whatToRemember: Features that only look like blemishes leave an animal fit for the מזבח. But they do not allow a בכור to be slaughtered outside the מקדש.

phrases.english: It was also taught so:
There are things that are like blemishes,
but are not like blemishes,
and we slaughter with them in the Temple,
but not in the country.
phrases.notes: A בכור with one of these features may not be slaughtered outside the מקדש.

phrases.english: And these are they:
a female goat that has no horns,
phrases.notes: The text in brackets is a correction of the reading in parentheses.

phrases.english: and a female lamb that has horns,
and the tzime'ach, the tzimem, and the tzime'a.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports רב חסדא's ruling with a ברייתא.
steps.raayaObject: רב חסדא's ruling that a hornless goat and a horned lamb are fit for the מזבח.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא that lists features that look like blemishes but are not real ones.

steps.title: Horns lost with their bone versus hooves lost with their bone
steps.stepSummary: רב חסדא quotes אמימר. If horns are removed with their inner bone, the animal is unfit but cannot be redeemed. If hooves are removed with their bone, the animal is unfit and can be redeemed.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חסדא said in the name of אמימר: If the horns were removed and their bone with them, the animal is unfit, but we do not redeem it because of that. If the hooves were removed and their bone with them, they are unfit and they are redeemed because of that.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new ruling about two kinds of damage: horns pulled off with their bone, and hooves pulled off with their bone.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There are two separate questions here. First, may the animal still go on the מזבח? Second, is this a full מום that lets you redeem a קדשים animal? Losing a horn with its bone answers 'no' to both. Losing a hoof with its bone counts as a full מום, so the animal may be redeemed.

keyTerms.meaning: An אמורא whose ruling רב חסדא reports here
The hard bone inside the horn or hoof
We redeem the animal because of this damage, which shows it is a full מום

steps.confusionAlert: 'Unfit' and 'can be redeemed' are not the same thing. An animal can be too damaged for the מזבח and still not have a real מום that permits פדיון.

phrases.english: Rav Chisda said that Ameimar said:
If their horns were removed, and their bones with them —
it is unfit, but we do not redeem it on account of them.
phrases.notes: It is not a full blemish.

phrases.english: If the hooves were removed, and their bones with them —
they are unfit, and they are redeemed on account of them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new ruling about horns, after the earlier discussion of animals with no horns.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Horns removed with their bone: the animal is unfit and cannot be redeemed. Hooves removed with their bone: the animal is unfit and can be redeemed.

steps.title: A ברייתא says lost horns also allow redemption
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא puts horns and hooves together. It says both make the animal unfit and both allow redemption. That contradicts רב חסדא about horns.
steps.simpleTranslation: They challenged him: If the horns or the hooves were removed and their bones with them, they are unfit and they are redeemed on account of them!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רב חסדא with a ברייתא that seems to give the opposite ruling about horns.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב חסדא said horns do not allow redemption. The ברייתא treats horns exactly like hooves and allows redemption for both. So the ruling on horns is under attack.

keyTerms.meaning: 'They challenged': an objection from a תנאי source

phrases.english: They raised an objection:
If the horns or the hooves were removed
and their bones with them —
they are unfit and are redeemed on account of them!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the horn half of step 36.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב חסדא's ruling that horns removed with their bone do not allow redemption
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא says horns, just like hooves, allow redemption.

steps.title: Uprooted versus cut
steps.stepSummary: There is no contradiction. The ברייתא is about a bone that was fully uprooted, which is a full מום. רב חסדא is about a bone that was only cut.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is not difficult. This ברייתא is where the bone was fully uprooted. That ruling of רב חסדא is where it was only cut.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by showing that the two sources are talking about two different cases.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the horn bone is pulled out completely, it is a full מום and the animal can be redeemed, as the ברייתא says. If the bone is only cut off, the animal is unfit but cannot be redeemed, as רב חסדא says. Both rulings stay true.

keyTerms.meaning: It is not difficult; this introduces an answer that splits the cases
It was cut off, not pulled out

phrases.english: It is not difficult:
this (the baraita) is where it was totally uprooted,
that (Rav Chisda) is where it was cut off.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 37.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases (אוקימתא): the two sources describe different kinds of damage
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא and רב חסדא both describe the same horn damage, so they contradict each other.
steps.terutzMaskana: Uprooting the bone is a full מום that allows redemption. Cutting the bone only makes the animal unfit.

steps.title: Does cutting a horn disqualify at all? The פרה אדומה
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא now asks whether a cut horn makes the animal unfit at all. A משנה says that if a פרה אדומה has black horns and hooves, you cut the black parts off. So cutting a horn does not seem to blemish the animal.
steps.simpleTranslation: And where it was only cut, is it really unfit? They contrasted it: A heifer whose horns and hooves are black, one should cut them off!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the answer it just gave by asking whether a cut horn makes the animal unfit at all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A פרה אדומה must be free of any מום. Yet the משנה tells us to cut off its black horns. If cutting a horn made an animal unfit, this cutting would ruin the פרה. So the challenge is to the claim that a cut horn makes the animal unfit.

keyTerms.meaning: 'And they contrasted': it shows that two sources contradict each other
The red heifer, which must be fully red and have no מום

phrases.english: And where it was cut off, is it unfit?
And they contrasted it:
A (red) heifer whose horns and hooves are black —
one should cut them off!
phrases.notes: The heifer stays valid, so cutting seems to cause no blemish.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the 'cut' case set up in step 38.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that a cut horn makes the animal unfit
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The משנה tells us to cut the horns of a פרה אדומה, which must have no מום, and it stays valid. So cutting a horn should not make an animal unfit.

steps.title: זעירי: the פרה is cut only above the bone
steps.stepSummary: זעירי explains that the פרה אדומה משנה means cutting the horn only above the inner bone. That does not disqualify. Cutting into the bone itself does.
steps.simpleTranslation: זעירי explained it: it means cutting from above the bone.
steps.whatsHappening: זעירי answers the challenge by explaining that the פרה אדומה case is a smaller kind of cut.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With the פרה אדומה, you trim only the outer horn above the bone, so no real damage is done. רב חסדא's case is where the bone itself is cut, and that makes the animal unfit. Both sources stand.

keyTerms.meaning: He explained it, often by limiting a source to a specific case

steps.whatToRemember: There are three levels of horn damage. Trimming above the bone: no problem at all, as with the פרה אדומה. Cutting the bone: unfit, but cannot be redeemed (רב חסדא). Uprooting the bone completely: a full מום, so the animal can be redeemed (the ברייתא).

phrases.english: Ze'eiri interpreted it:
from above the bone.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 39.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases (אוקימתא): the פרה אדומה cut is above the bone
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Cutting the horns of the פרה means the same cut as רב חסדא's case.
steps.terutzMaskana: Trimming above the bone causes no מום. Cutting the bone itself makes the animal unfit.
